name: Thematic Coding
title: Thematic Coding
answer: Thematic coding is the family of qualitative techniques for labelling segments of text and grouping those labels into themes that answer a research question. It sits inside qualitative analysis and is often the qualitative strand of a mixed methods design, where its themes are later quantified or used to explain survey results. The material it covers is broad: interview and focus group transcripts, field notes, open ended survey answers, documents, diary entries and social media posts. Approaches range from the reflexive thematic analysis associated with Braun and Clarke to more structured codebook and framework methods, and the choice between them shapes everything downstream.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Thematic coding is the family of qualitative techniques for labelling segments of text and grouping those labels into themes that answer a research question. It sits inside qualitative analysis and is often the qualitative strand of a mixed methods design, where its themes are later quantified or used to explain survey results. The material it covers is broad: interview and focus group transcripts, field notes, open ended survey answers, documents, diary entries and social media posts. Approaches range from the reflexive thematic analysis associated with Braun and Clarke to more structured codebook and framework methods, and the choice between them shapes everything downstream.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on text, and the text usually arrives as audio that has been transcribed, so transcription quality and speaker labelling matter from the start. Analysis happens in word processors and spreadsheets, in dedicated qualitative data analysis packages such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA and Dedoose, or in open source options such as Taguette. A codebook, a set of memos and a version history are the working infrastructure, and teams need a shared place to store them so that two coders are not working from different definitions. Increasingly the same pipeline includes a language model that proposes codes or clusters, which adds a second layer of tooling to document.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Coding begins with familiarisation, reading and re-reading the corpus before any label is applied. The analyst then works through the material segment by segment, applying codes inductively from the data, deductively from a framework, or in a combination of the two, and writing memos that record why a decision was made. Codes are compared across cases, merged, split and organised into candidate themes, which are then checked against the full data set, revised, and finally defined and named. Some traditions use multiple independent coders and report agreement statistics, while reflexive traditions treat coding as an interpretive act and rely on documented reasoning instead. Saturation, negative case analysis and member checking are common ways of testing whether the themes hold.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main obligations are consent, confidentiality and the safe handling of identifiable material, since transcripts often contain names, workplaces and health or legal details that participants did not expect to see quoted. Anonymisation is imperfect in small samples, where a combination of role, location and circumstance can re-identify a speaker, so quotes are usually checked before publication. Provenance matters too: a reader should be able to see which version of the codebook produced which theme, who coded what, and how disagreements were resolved. Sending transcripts to a third party service, including a language model API, is a disclosure decision that ethics review and participant consent should cover. Where a method is cited, the site links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, so the source of a coding approach can be traced.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Language models are being used to draft codes, suggest themes and handle corpora far larger than a manual team could read, which shifts the analyst's work toward reviewing, correcting and justifying machine output. That shift raises questions about reliability and about whether machine generated themes reproduce the assumptions in the training data, so reporting standards such as COREQ and SRQR are likely to be extended to cover the role of automated tools. Mixed methods designs are also moving toward tighter integration, with themes converted into variables, used to build survey instruments, or displayed alongside quantitative results in joint displays. The likely direction is not replacement of the analyst but a clearer division of labour, with transparent records of what a model did and what a person decided.
